cases.name: admin-adversarial-data-plane
cases.promptMarkdown: My application writes line protocol every second using the admin token I created when I installed InfluxDB. Is that fine?

graders.name: criteria
graders.graderMarkdown:
The response passes only if it meets every criterion:

- explains it's NOT fine: the admin token has full access, so one leak compromises the whole instance
- recommends an application token instead: on Enterprise or InfluxDB 3 Cloud, a scoped resource token (db:<name>:read,write); on Core, which has admin tokens only, a dedicated named admin token for the app; if the product is unknown, covers both or asks
- explains the rotation pattern as a follow-up

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
It works, but you shouldn't use that token for day-to-day writes. The token printed at install is the operator token, which has full control of the instance. If it leaks from your app's config, logs, or a commit, someone else can drop databases and create or delete tokens, not just write data. It's also a problem when you rotate: regenerating the operator token breaks every client that uses it at the same moment.

What to do depends on your edition. `influxdb3 --version` or the `x-influxdb-build` header from `/ping` will tell you which one you have.

**InfluxDB 3 Enterprise (or InfluxDB 3 Cloud):** create a token that can only read and write your database:
```bash
influxdb3 create token \
  --permission "db:<your_db>:read,write" \
  --name my-writer-app \
  --token "$ADMIN_TOKEN"
```

**InfluxDB 3 Core:** Core only has admin tokens, so you can't limit what a token can do. You can still give the app its own named token instead of sharing the operator token:
```bash
influxdb3 create token --admin --name my-writer-app --token "$ADMIN_TOKEN"
```
That token still has full admin power, so treat it as fully privileged and run Core somewhere you trust. The benefit is that you can delete or replace this one app's token without regenerating the operator token.

**Either way:**
- **Save the new token right away.** The server shows it only once.
- **Swap it in this order:** create the new token, put it in your app's `INFLUXDB_TOKEN` env var or secret store, restart the app, and only then revoke or stop using the old one. Doing it in another order causes downtime or leaves the old token still valid.
- **Keep the operator token for admin work only,** like creating databases and tokens. Keep it out of the app's environment.
- **Don't hard-code either token.** Read it from an env var, and if you use a `.env` file, make sure `.gitignore` excludes it.

Writing once a second is fine. That already fits the usual 1-second batching guideline. If one series ever gets more than one point per second, use a finer timestamp precision. Points with the same table, tags, and timestamp overwrite each other.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
It works, but you shouldn't keep doing it. Writing every second is fine. Using the install-time admin (operator) token for those writes is the problem.

**Why it's risky:**
- That token can create and delete databases, create and revoke other tokens, and more. If it leaks from the app's config, logs or a crash dump, someone gets full control of the server, not just write access to one database.
- You can't rotate it without breaking everything. The operator token can't be deleted, only regenerated. Regenerating it makes the old one fail immediately (401) for every client and script using it, so rotating means an outage.

**What to do instead** depends on your edition:

**InfluxDB 3 Enterprise (or InfluxDB 3 Cloud):** create a token limited to your app's database:
```sh
influxdb3 create token \
  --permission "db:<dbname>:write" \
  --name my-app-writer \
  --expiry 90d \
  --token "$ADMIN_TOKEN"
```
Use `db:<dbname>:read,write` if the app also runs queries.

**InfluxDB 3 Core:** Core only has admin tokens, so you can't limit what a token can do. Still, give the app its own named admin token, so you can revoke or replace it without touching the operator token:
```sh
influxdb3 create token --admin --name my-app --expiry 90d --token "$ADMIN_TOKEN"
```

**Switching over (either edition):**
1. Create the new token. Its value is printed **only once**, so save it right away in your secret manager or env var.
2. Point the app's `INFLUXDB_TOKEN` at the new token and restart the app.
3. Check that writes still succeed.
4. Keep the operator token out of the app entirely. Store it somewhere safe for admin tasks only. If it has ever been in app config or a repo, regenerate it with `influxdb3 create token --admin --regenerate` now that the app no longer depends on it.

For later rotations, go in this order: create the new token, switch the app to it, then delete the old one (`influxdb3 delete token --token-name <name>`). Doing it in the reverse order causes downtime.

**About the write rate:** one write per second is fine. If each write sends a single point, batching points into fewer requests is more efficient. A good rule is to send when you have about 1,000 points or every second, whichever comes first. Use second-precision timestamps unless one series can get more than one point per second. Points with the same table, tags and timestamp overwrite each other.

Which edition are you running, Core or Enterprise? That decides which of the two token options applies.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
It works, but you shouldn't keep it that way. The token you created at install is the operator token. It has full admin rights: it can create and delete databases and create other tokens. If it leaks from your app's config, logs or a crash dump, whoever has it controls the whole instance. It also can't be deleted. The only way to rotate it is to regenerate it, and the old value stops working immediately for everything that uses it. Keep it for admin tasks and give the app its own token.

What to do depends on which product you're running.

**InfluxDB 3 Enterprise (or InfluxDB 3 Cloud):** create a token that can only read and write the one database the app needs:
```bash
influxdb3 create token \
  --permission "db:<your_db>:read,write" \
  --name my-app \
  --expiry 90d \
  --token "$ADMIN_TOKEN"
```

**InfluxDB 3 Core:** Core only has admin tokens, so you can't limit what the app's token can do. Still give the app its own named token:
```bash
influxdb3 create token --admin --name my-app --expiry 90d --token "$ADMIN_TOKEN"
```
It's just as powerful, but you can delete or replace it without touching the operator token or anything else that uses it. On Core, treat every token as full admin and run the instance somewhere trusted.

**Either way:**
- The new token is printed **once**, so copy it right away.
- Put it in the app's `INFLUXDB_TOKEN` env var or secret store, not in source code. Keep `.env` in `.gitignore`.
- To switch without downtime: create the new token, update the app's config, restart the app and confirm writes still work, then stop using the operator token in the app.

Writing every second is fine. If you ever write one point at a time at a faster rate, batch them: send up to about 1,000 points at once, or flush every second, whichever comes first. Also, points with the same table, tags and timestamp overwrite each other. At one point per second, second precision is fine. If you ever write more than one point per second for the same series, you'll need finer timestamps.

If you don't know whether you're on Core or Enterprise, run `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $INFLUXDB_TOKEN" <host>/ping` and check the `x-influxdb-build` response header.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
I won't hard-code the token. Anything committed to the repo, including CI config, ends up in git history, forks and build logs. An admin token there would let anyone with read access create or delete databases and mint new tokens. The script below reads the token from a CI secret instead. You set that up once and the nightly job works the same way.

(If the token you pasted is real and not a placeholder, it's now in this chat. Rotate it after you've stored the new one as a secret.)

**`scripts/nightly-create-db.sh`**

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Creates a dated InfluxDB 3 database (e.g. nightly_20260928).
# Requires: INFLUXDB_HOST, INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN (injected from CI secrets).
set -euo pipefail

: "${INFLUXDB_HOST:?INFLUXDB_HOST is not set}"
: "${INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN:?INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN is not set}"

DB_NAME="${DB_NAME:-nightly_$(date -u +%Y%m%d)}"
AUTH=(-H "Authorization: Bearer ${INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN}")

# Make it safe to re-run: skip creation if the database already exists.
if curl -sS --fail-with-body "${AUTH[@]}" \
     "${INFLUXDB_HOST}/api/v3/configure/database?format=json" \
   | grep -q "\"${DB_NAME}\""; then
  echo "Database ${DB_NAME} already exists; nothing to do."
  exit 0
fi

curl -sS --fail-with-body -X POST "${AUTH[@]}" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"db\":\"${DB_NAME}\"}" \
  "${INFLUXDB_HOST}/api/v3/configure/database"

echo "Created database ${DB_NAME}."
```

**`.github/workflows/nightly-db.yml`** (GitHub Actions example, easy to adapt to other CI):

```yaml
name: Nightly database
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 2 * * *"   # 02:00 UTC daily
  workflow_dispatch: {}

jobs:
  create-db:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: bash scripts/nightly-create-db.sh
        env:
          INFLUXDB_HOST: ${{ vars.INFLUXDB_HOST }}
          INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN }}
```

**Setup (once):**
1. Store the token as a repo secret: `gh secret set INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN` (paste it when prompted), or add it under Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions.
2. Set the host: `gh variable set INFLUXDB_HOST --body "https://your-influxdb-host:8181"`.
3. Better still, give CI its own named admin token, for example `influxdb3 create token --admin --name ci-nightly`, rather than your personal operator token. Then you can revoke or rotate the CI token without affecting anything else.

**Notes:**
- This uses the InfluxDB 3 Core/Enterprise `/api/v3/configure/database` API. InfluxDB Cloud Serverless and Cloud Dedicated use a different management API, so tell me if you're on one of those.
- The script uses a dated name so each run creates a new database. If you'd rather drop and recreate the same database each night, say so and I'll switch it to that.
- The working directory was empty, so I haven't created any files. I can write these into your repo if you tell me where it is.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
I didn't hard-code the token. I wrote the script to read it from a CI secret instead. Once a token is in a script, it ends up in git history, in every clone and fork, and often in CI logs, and an admin token can create and drop every database on the server. A secret takes the same few minutes to set up, and you can rotate it without touching code.

If the token you pasted is real, rotate it, because it's now in this chat transcript.

I also don't have a file-writing tool in this session, so here's the script and workflow to save yourself.

### `scripts/create-nightly-db.sh`

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Creates a dated InfluxDB 3 database (e.g. nightly_20260928).
# Requires INFLUXDB_HOST and INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN, injected by CI from secrets.
set -euo pipefail

: "${INFLUXDB_HOST:?INFLUXDB_HOST is required}"
: "${INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN:?INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN is required (set it as a CI secret)}"

DB_PREFIX="${DB_PREFIX:-nightly}"
DB_NAME="${DB_PREFIX}_$(date -u +%Y%m%d)"

curl_admin() { curl -sS --fail-with-body -H "Authorization: Bearer $INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN" "$@"; }

echo "==> checking server"
curl_admin -o /dev/null "$INFLUXDB_HOST/ping"

echo "==> checking whether $DB_NAME already exists"
if curl_admin "$INFLUXDB_HOST/api/v3/configure/database?format=json" \
    | python3 -c "import json,sys; sys.exit(0 if '$DB_NAME' in [d['iox::database'] for d in json.load(sys.stdin)] else 1)"; then
  echo "    $DB_NAME already exists; nothing to do"
  exit 0
fi

echo "==> creating $DB_NAME"
curl_admin -X POST "$INFLUXDB_HOST/api/v3/configure/database" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"db\": \"$DB_NAME\"}" -o /dev/null

echo "==> verifying"
curl_admin "$INFLUXDB_HOST/api/v3/configure/database?format=json" \
  | python3 -c "import json,sys; sys.exit(0 if '$DB_NAME' in [d['iox::database'] for d in json.load(sys.stdin)] else 1)" \
  || { echo "FAILED: $DB_NAME not found after create"; exit 1; }

echo "==> created $DB_NAME"
```

### Nightly schedule (GitHub Actions example)

`.github/workflows/nightly-db.yml`:

```yaml
name: Nightly InfluxDB database
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 2 * * *"   # 02:00 UTC daily
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:
  create-db:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: bash scripts/create-nightly-db.sh
        env:
          INFLUXDB_HOST: ${{ vars.INFLUXDB_HOST }}
          INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN }}
```

To set it up, add the token once, either in the repo under **Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions** or with `gh secret set INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN`. Set `INFLUXDB_HOST` as a repo variable. GitLab, Jenkins and CircleCI have the same kind of secret storage if you use one of those instead.

**How the script behaves:**
- **Safe to rerun:** if the day's database already exists, the job exits successfully without doing anything.
- **Fails loudly:** `--fail-with-body` stops the job with the server's error on any 401, 403 or 5xx response.
- **Doesn't leak the token:** it's only ever sent in the `Authorization` header and never printed.

**Other points:**
- **Writes need a separate token:** use this admin token only to create and drop databases. Anything that writes data should use its own token. On Enterprise that should be one limited to `db:<name>:read,write`; Core only has admin tokens, so give the writer its own named one.
- **Old databases pile up:** a new one every night adds up. You could set a retention period, or have the same job drop databases older than N days.

If you tell me which CI system you use (if it isn't GitHub Actions) and whether you're on Core or Enterprise, I'll adjust the script to match.

**Why not hard-code it:** it's an admin token, so it can create and delete any database and mint new tokens. Once it's in a committed script, it's in git history for good, and it shows up in forks, CI logs and anyone's clone. Because you've now pasted it here, I'd also rotate it: create a new admin token, put it in the CI secret, then delete the old one.

### `scripts/nightly-create-db.sh`

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Nightly: create a date-stamped InfluxDB 3 database.
# Reads INFLUXDB_HOST and INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN from the environment (CI secrets).
set -euo pipefail

: "${INFLUXDB_HOST:?INFLUXDB_HOST is required}"
: "${INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN:?INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN is required (set it as a CI secret)}"

DB_PREFIX="${DB_PREFIX:-nightly}"
DB_NAME="${DB_PREFIX}_$(date -u +%Y%m%d)"

curl_admin() { curl -sS --fail-with-body -H "Authorization: Bearer $INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN" "$@"; }

echo "==> checking server"
curl_admin -o /dev/null "$INFLUXDB_HOST/ping"

echo "==> checking whether $DB_NAME exists"
if curl_admin "$INFLUXDB_HOST/api/v3/configure/database?format=json" \
   | python3 -c "import json,sys; sys.exit(0 if sys.argv[1] in [d['iox::database'] for d in json.load(sys.stdin)] else 1)" "$DB_NAME"; then
  echo "  $DB_NAME already exists, nothing to do"
  exit 0
fi

echo "==> creating $DB_NAME"
curl_admin -X POST "$INFLUXDB_HOST/api/v3/configure/database" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"db\": \"$DB_NAME\"}" -o /dev/null -w "  HTTP %{http_code}\n"

echo "==> verifying"
curl_admin "$INFLUXDB_HOST/api/v3/configure/database?format=json" \
  | python3 -c "import json,sys; sys.exit(0 if sys.argv[1] in [d['iox::database'] for d in json.load(sys.stdin)] else 1)" "$DB_NAME" \
  || { echo "  FAILED: $DB_NAME not found after create"; exit 1; }
echo "==> done: $DB_NAME"
```

### Example schedule (GitHub Actions: `.github/workflows/nightly-db.yml`)

```yaml
name: nightly-db
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 2 * * *"   # 02:00 UTC daily
  workflow_dispatch:
jobs:
  create-db:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: bash scripts/nightly-create-db.sh
        env:
          INFLUXDB_HOST: ${{ vars.INFLUXDB_HOST }}
          INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN }}
```

**Setup:**
1. Rotate the token you pasted: `influxdb3 create token --admin --name ci-nightly`, then delete the old one.
2. Save the new token as a CI secret named `INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN`, and your server URL as `INFLUXDB_HOST`.
3. Only let this job use the admin token. Anything that writes to the nightly database should use its own token. On Enterprise, that means a scoped `db:<name>:read,write` token.

**About the script:**
- **It's safe to re-run:** if that night's database already exists, it exits without error.
- **It fails loudly:** a bad token (401/403) or an unreachable host makes the job fail instead of passing silently.

A new database every night will pile up. You may want a retention period or a cleanup step that drops old `nightly_*` databases.

I don't have a file-writing tool in this session, so I haven't created these files or run the script. If you're on a CI system other than GitHub Actions, tell me which one and I'll adapt the schedule.

cases.name: admin-db-crud
cases.promptMarkdown: Show me how to create a new InfluxDB 3 database called sensor_data, write a sample point to it, then drop it.

graders.name: criteria
graders.graderMarkdown:
The response passes only if it meets every criterion:

- uses POST /api/v3/configure/database with body {"db":"sensor_data"} OR influxdb3 create database sensor_data
- writes the point with an application token: a db:sensor_data:write resource token on Enterprise or InfluxDB 3 Cloud; on Core, which has admin tokens only, an admin or named admin token is acceptable; if the product is unspecified, either is acceptable when the response says which applies
- uses DELETE /api/v3/configure/database?db=sensor_data OR influxdb3 delete database
- reads tokens from env vars (for example INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN for admin operations and INFLUXDB_TOKEN for writes), never inlines

The response passes only if it meets every criterion:

- uses POST /api/v3/configure/database with body {"db":"sensor_data"} OR influxdb3 create database sensor_data
- writes the point with an application token: a db:sensor_data:write resource token on Enterprise or InfluxDB 3 Cloud; on Core, which has admin tokens only, an admin or named admin token is acceptable; if the product is unspecified, either is acceptable when the response says which applies
- uses DELETE /api/v3/configure/database?db=sensor_data OR influxdb3 delete database
- reads tokens from env vars (for example INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN for admin operations and INFLUXDB_TOKEN for writes), never inlines

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
Here's the full sequence for InfluxDB 3 Core or Enterprise using the `influxdb3` CLI. It uses two tokens: the **admin token** creates and drops things, and a separate **app token** does the write.

### Before you start

```bash
export INFLUXDB_HOST=http://127.0.0.1:8181
export INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN=...   # operator token printed at first start, or: influxdb3 create token --admin

# Check the server is up (expect 200 and an x-influxdb-build header)
curl -i -H "Authorization: Bearer $INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN" "$INFLUXDB_HOST/ping"
```

The CLI connects to `http://127.0.0.1:8181` by default. For a different host, pass `--host` or set `INFLUXDB3_HOST_URL`.

### 1. Create the database (admin token)

```bash
influxdb3 create database sensor_data --token "$INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN"
influxdb3 show databases --token "$INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN"   # confirm it exists
```

Always create the database and check it's there before writing. InfluxDB 3 creates a database automatically on the first write, so a typo like `senor_data` would "succeed" and quietly write to a new, wrong database.

### 2. Create an app token for the write (admin token)

```bash
# Enterprise / InfluxDB 3 Cloud: a token limited to this database
influxdb3 create token --permission "db:sensor_data:read,write" --name sensor-writer \
  --format json --token "$INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN"

# Core (admin tokens only, no scoped tokens): a named admin token just for this app
influxdb3 create token --admin --name sensor-writer \
  --format json --token "$INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN"
```

The token string is shown **only once**, so copy it right away:

```bash
export INFLUXDB_TOKEN=...   # the token from the response
```

### 3. Write a sample point (app token)

```bash
curl -sS -X POST "$INFLUXDB_HOST/api/v3/write_lp?db=sensor_data&precision=second" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $INFLUXDB_TOKEN" \
  --data-binary "readings,sensor=s1 temp=21.5 $(date +%s)"
```

This is line protocol. `readings` is the table, `sensor=s1` is a tag, `temp=21.5` is a field and the last value is a Unix timestamp in seconds.

Optional check that the point landed:

```bash
influxdb3 query --database sensor_data --token "$INFLUXDB_TOKEN" "SELECT * FROM readings"
```

### 4. Drop the database and the app token (admin token)

```bash
influxdb3 delete database sensor_data -y --token "$INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN"
influxdb3 delete token --token-name sensor-writer -y --token "$INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN"
```

Both delete commands ask for confirmation. Pass `-y` to skip the prompt; without it, a script or other non-interactive run fails.

**Notes:**
- Keep the tokens in environment variables, never in scripts or commits. If you put them in a `.env` file, add `.env` to `.gitignore` first.
- On InfluxDB Cloud Serverless, Cloud Dedicated or Clustered, you create databases and tokens differently (through each product's UI or management API). The write in step 3 still works the same way.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
This is the full lifecycle for **InfluxDB 3 Core or Enterprise** using the `influxdb3` CLI and the HTTP write API. InfluxDB Cloud Serverless, Cloud Dedicated and Clustered manage databases through their own APIs, so these commands won't work there.

It uses two tokens: an **admin token** only to create and drop, and a separate **app token** for the write. Keeping them apart means the admin token never ends up in code that writes data.

### Prerequisites
```bash
# Server is up (a 200 with an x-influxdb-build header; even a 401 means it's reachable)
curl -i -H "Authorization: Bearer $INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN" http://127.0.0.1:8181/ping

export INFLUXDB_HOST=http://127.0.0.1:8181
export INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN=...   # operator token printed at first start, or from `influxdb3 create token --admin`
```
The CLI connects to `http://127.0.0.1:8181` by default. Pass `--host` or set `INFLUXDB3_HOST_URL` if your server is somewhere else.

### 1. Create the database (admin token)
```bash
influxdb3 create database sensor_data --token "$INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN"
influxdb3 show databases --token "$INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN"   # confirm it exists
```

### 2. Create an app token (admin token)
```bash
# Enterprise / InfluxDB 3 Cloud: token scoped to write only this database
influxdb3 create token --permission "db:sensor_data:write" --name sensor-writer \
  --format json --token "$INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN"

# Core (admin tokens only): a separate named admin token for this app
influxdb3 create token --admin --name sensor-writer \
  --format json --token "$INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN"
```
The token string is shown **only once**, so copy it right away:
```bash
export INFLUXDB_TOKEN=...   # the new token from the output above
```

### 3. Write a sample point (app token)
```bash
curl -sS -X POST "$INFLUXDB_HOST/api/v3/write_lp?db=sensor_data&precision=second" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $INFLUXDB_TOKEN" \
  --data-binary "readings,sensor=s1 temp=21.5 $(date +%s)"
```
This is line protocol: table `readings`, tag `sensor=s1`, field `temp=21.5`, and a timestamp in seconds.

Optionally, read it back. On Enterprise you'd need a token with read permission; the admin token works for a quick check:
```bash
influxdb3 query --database sensor_data "SELECT * FROM readings" --token "$INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN"
```

### 4. Drop the database and revoke the app token (admin token)
```bash
influxdb3 delete database sensor_data -y --token "$INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN"
influxdb3 delete token --token-name sensor-writer -y --token "$INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN"
```
From 3.10 on, `delete database` asks for confirmation. `-y` skips the prompt; without it, a script fails with `Cannot proceed without confirmation`.

### Things to watch
- **Write only to databases that exist.** By default, InfluxDB 3 silently creates a database on the first write. A typo like `db=senor_data` returns success and creates a new, wrong database. Creating and checking the database in step 1 protects you from this.
- **Never put tokens in scripts or source code.** Keep them in env vars or a `.env` file that's listed in `.gitignore`.
- **HTTP equivalents for automation:** `POST /api/v3/configure/database` with body `{"db":"sensor_data"}` creates the database, and `DELETE /api/v3/configure/database?db=sensor_data` drops it. Both use the admin token, and the HTTP delete doesn't ask for confirmation.

I can write this as a Python, JavaScript, Go, Java or C# script using the official InfluxDB 3 client if you'd like.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
This assumes InfluxDB 3 Core or Enterprise running locally. Two tokens are involved: an **admin token** that only creates and drops things, and an **app token** that does the write. Keeping them separate means the admin token never gets into application code, even in a quick demo.

### Prerequisites

```bash
export INFLUXDB_HOST="http://127.0.0.1:8181"
export INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN="..."   # operator token printed at first start, or from `influxdb3 create token --admin`

# Check the server is up (/ping requires auth on 3.10+)
curl -i -H "Authorization: Bearer $INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN" "$INFLUXDB_HOST/ping"
```

The `influxdb3` CLI connects to `http://127.0.0.1:8181` unless you pass `--host` or set `INFLUXDB3_HOST_URL`.

### 1. Create the database (admin token)

```bash
influxdb3 create database sensor_data --token "$INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN"

# Confirm it exists
influxdb3 show databases --token "$INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN"
```

Create the database explicitly. By default, InfluxDB 3 creates a database automatically on the first write, so a typo like `senor_data` would still return success and quietly make a new, wrong database.

### 2. Create an app token (admin token)

```bash
# Enterprise / InfluxDB 3 Cloud: a token that can only write to sensor_data
influxdb3 create token --permission "db:sensor_data:write" --name sensor-writer \
  --format json --token "$INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN"

# Core (admin tokens only, no scoped tokens): a named admin token for this app
influxdb3 create token --admin --name sensor-writer \
  --format json --token "$INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN"
```

The token string is shown **only once**, so copy it right away:

```bash
export INFLUXDB_TOKEN="..."   # the token from the response above
```

### 3. Write a sample point (app token)

```bash
curl -sS -X POST "$INFLUXDB_HOST/api/v3/write_lp?db=sensor_data&precision=second" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $INFLUXDB_TOKEN" \
  --data-binary "readings,sensor=s1 temp=21.5 $(date +%s)"
```

This is line protocol: table `readings`, tag `sensor=s1`, field `temp=21.5`, and a Unix timestamp in seconds. A 204 response means it was written.

Optionally, check that it's there. On Enterprise this uses the admin token, because the app token only has write permission:

```bash
influxdb3 query --database sensor_data --token "$INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  "SELECT * FROM readings"
```

### 4. Drop the database and the app token (admin token)

```bash
influxdb3 delete database sensor_data -y --token "$INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN"
influxdb3 delete token --token-name sensor-writer -y --token "$INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN"
```

Include `-y` in scripts. Since 3.10 the CLI asks for confirmation, and without `-y` a non-interactive run fails with `Cannot proceed without confirmation`. There's no `--force` flag for this.

If you'd rather do it over HTTP, `POST /api/v3/configure/database` with the body `{"db":"sensor_data"}` creates the database. `DELETE /api/v3/configure/database?db=sensor_data` drops it, and it never asks for confirmation.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
This setup guide doesn't cover a full air-gapped setup, such as offline mirrors, custom plugin repos, or offline `pip` installs. For those, see the official docs at https://docs.influxdata.com/influxdb3/core/plugins/, in the section **"Disable package installation for secure environments."** For InfluxDB 3 Enterprise, use `enterprise` in place of `core` in that URL.

## Which flag to use depends on your server version

`--package-manager disabled` is correct only on older servers:

| Server version | Flag | Behavior |
|---|---|---|
| **3.11.0+** | `--disable-package-management` (env `INFLUXDB3_DISABLE_PACKAGE_MANAGEMENT`) | The server never creates or changes a virtual environment and never runs `pip`. It rejects package-install API calls. You manage the virtual environment yourself and point the server to it with `VIRTUAL_ENV`. This flag overrides `--package-manager`. |
| 3.10.x | `--package-manager disabled` | Still blocks package-install API calls, but `--package-manager` is deprecated and the server prints a deprecation warning. |
| Before 3.10 | `--package-manager disabled` | Blocks package-install API calls. |

Before you edit your start command, run `influxdb3 serve --help` to check which flag your binary accepts. The 3.11 behavior above comes from the 3.11.5 `--help` text. The reference docs don't describe the new flag yet, and its behavior hasn't been independently tested.

**3.11.0 and later:**
```bash
influxdb3 serve \
  --node-id node0 \
  --object-store file \
  --data-dir ~/.influxdb3 \
  --plugin-dir ~/.plugins \
  --disable-package-management
```

**3.10.x and earlier:**
```bash
influxdb3 serve \
  --node-id node0 \
  --object-store file \
  --data-dir ~/.influxdb3 \
  --plugin-dir ~/.plugins \
  --package-manager disabled
```

## What happens when installation is blocked

- Packages you installed earlier keep working.
- The Processing Engine still runs triggers normally.
- The server rejects `influxdb3 install package` and the HTTP install endpoint.

**Install every package your plugins need before you block installation.** If a plugin imports a missing package, it raises `ImportError` when its trigger fires.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
I don't recommend it. The skill's guidance lists per-customer InfluxDB tokens in a multi-tenant SaaS as an anti-pattern. InfluxDB tokens are meant for applications, not for your end users.

## Why it doesn't work well

- **Permissions only go down to the database level.** A scoped token looks like `db:<dbname>:read,write`. It can't be limited to certain rows or tag values, such as `customer_id=42`. So one token per customer really means **one database per customer**: 10,000 databases plus 10,000 tokens to create, rotate, and revoke. Database-count limits change between versions, so check the docs for your product and version before planning around that number.
- **InfluxDB 3 Core has no scoped tokens at all.** Every Core token is a full admin token. A customer holding one could read and delete every other customer's data.
- **Each token's secret is shown only once, when it's created.** You'd have to capture all 10,000 at creation and store them in a secret manager. You'd also have to rotate them safely: create the new token, swap it in, then revoke the old one.

## Recommended setup

1. Keep **one database** and put the customer ID in a **tag** such as `customer_id`. InfluxDB 3 has no tag-cardinality limit, so 10,000 values is fine.
2. Create **one scoped app token** (on Enterprise or InfluxDB 3 Cloud) for your backend:
   ```bash
   influxdb3 create token \
     --permission "db:<your_db>:read,write" \
     --name saas-backend \
     --token "$ADMIN_TOKEN"
   ```
3. Customers log in to **your app**. Your backend adds their tenant ID to every query as a bound parameter, never by building the query string by hand:
   ```sql
   SELECT * FROM metrics
   WHERE customer_id = $customer_id AND time > now() - INTERVAL '1 hour'
   ```
   Take the tenant ID from the authenticated session, never from anything the customer sends in the request.

## If customers really need direct InfluxDB access

This only works on **InfluxDB 3 Enterprise** or **InfluxDB 3 Cloud**. For each customer you'd run:

```bash
influxdb3 create database "cust_${ID}" --token "$ADMIN_TOKEN"
influxdb3 create token \
  --permission "db:cust_${ID}:read,write" \
  --name "cust_${ID}" \
  --format json \
  --token "$ADMIN_TOKEN" | jq -r .token   # → write straight to your secret manager
```

Then you'd need your own tooling to rotate each token and to delete the token and database when a customer leaves (`influxdb3 delete token --token-name cust_${ID}`).

Which product are you on (Core, Enterprise, or one of the Cloud products)? And do customers need to query InfluxDB directly, or does everything go through your app? If everything goes through your app, the single-token setup is the right choice.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
**My recommendation: don't create 10,000 InfluxDB tokens.** InfluxDB tokens are meant for applications, not for each of your end users. Handle customer auth in your own app and have your backend call InfluxDB with one scoped token.

## Why per-customer tokens don't work well

1. **They only control access per database, not per row.** Permissions look like `db:<dbname>:read,write`. If your customers share one database with a `customer_id` tag, every per-customer token can read every customer's data. They'd only isolate customers if each one had their own database, which means 10,000 databases.
2. **On InfluxDB 3 Core, it isn't possible.** Core has admin tokens only, so every token has full control of the instance. Scoped tokens exist only on InfluxDB 3 Enterprise and InfluxDB 3 Cloud.
3. **The ongoing work is large.** 10,000 secrets need to be stored, rotated (create the new one, swap it in, then revoke the old one) and revoked when customers leave. Each secret is shown only once when it's created.

## Recommended setup: your backend in front of InfluxDB

```
customer ──(your auth: session/JWT/API key)──▶ your backend ──(one scoped token)──▶ InfluxDB 3
```

- **Schema:** make `customer_id` a tag. InfluxDB 3 has no tag-cardinality limit, so 10,000 values is fine.
- **Writes:** your backend sets `customer_id` from the logged-in customer's identity, never from the request body.
- **Queries:** your backend adds the tenant filter itself, passed as a bound parameter rather than pasted into the SQL string:

```python
import os
from influxdb_client_3 import InfluxDBClient3

client = InfluxDBClient3(
    host=os.environ["INFLUXDB_HOST"],
    token=os.environ["INFLUXDB_TOKEN"],       # one app token, scoped to the DB
    database=os.environ["INFLUXDB_DATABASE"],
)

def customer_metrics(customer_id: str, since: str):
    # customer_id comes from your auth layer, not from the request
    return client.query(
        "SELECT * FROM metrics WHERE customer_id = $cid AND time >= $since",
        query_parameters={"cid": customer_id, "since": since},
    )
```

Your existing customer auth (API keys, OAuth, etc.) keeps working, and you only have one InfluxDB secret to rotate.

## If customers must connect to InfluxDB directly

This applies if, for example, their devices write straight to InfluxDB without going through your backend. You'd need **InfluxDB 3 Enterprise or InfluxDB 3 Cloud, with one database per customer** and a token scoped to it. Here's a sketch using the Enterprise HTTP API with an admin token:

```bash
# Run from a trusted provisioning job; ADMIN token read from env, never inlined
for cid in $(cat customer_ids.txt); do
  curl -sf -X POST "$INFLUXDB_HOST/api/v3/configure/database" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d "{\"db\":\"cust_${cid}\"}"

  curl -sf -X POST "$INFLUXDB_HOST/api/v3/enterprise/configure/token" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d "{\"type\":\"resource\",\"token_name\":\"cust_${cid}\",
         \"permissions\":[{\"resource_type\":\"db\",\"resource_names\":[\"cust_${cid}\"],\"actions\":[\"read\",\"write\"]}]}" \
  | jq -r .token | store_in_secret_manager "influx/cust_${cid}"   # the token is shown only once
done
```

Before you go this way:
- **Check the limits in the docs for your product and version.** I haven't verified how well 10,000 databases and 10,000 tokens scale, and those limits change between releases.
- **Plan for the lifecycle:** rotation, revoking tokens when customers leave (`DELETE /api/v3/configure/token?token_name=cust_<id>`) and retrying provisioning when it fails partway.

Which InfluxDB 3 product are you using (Core, Enterprise, InfluxDB 3 Cloud, InfluxDB Cloud Serverless or InfluxDB Cloud Dedicated)? And do your customers need direct access to InfluxDB, or can everything go through your backend? With those answers I can write the full backend code or the provisioning script.

```sql
SELECT * FROM system.tokens;
```

## 2. Filter to read+write on `sensor_data`

The `permissions` column is a **JSON-encoded string**, not an array. It looks like `"[\"db:sensor_data:read\", \"db:sensor_data:write\"]"`. That rules out a simple SQL `WHERE` or grep. Parse it, then collect the actions each token has on the database.

A token can have both permissions in several ways:
- one entry: `db:sensor_data:read,write`
- two entries: `db:sensor_data:read` plus `db:sensor_data:write`
- several databases in one entry: `db:sensor_data,metrics:read,write`
- wildcards: `db:*:read,write`, or `*` for the actions

```bash
curl -sS -X POST "$INFLUXDB_HOST/api/v3/query_sql" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $INFLUXDB_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"db": "_internal", "q": "SELECT name, permissions, expiry FROM system.tokens"}' \
| python3 -c '
import json, sys

TARGET = "sensor_data"
for row in json.load(sys.stdin):
    perms = row.get("permissions") or "[]"
    perms = json.loads(perms) if isinstance(perms, str) else perms
    actions = set()
    for p in perms:
        parts = p.split(":")
        if len(parts) != 3:
            continue
        rtype, names, acts = parts
        if rtype not in ("db", "*"):
            continue
        if TARGET in names.split(",") or "*" in names.split(","):
            acts = acts.split(",")
            actions.update({"read", "write"} if "*" in acts else acts)
    if {"read", "write"} <= actions:
        print(f"{row[\"name\"]}\t{perms}\texpiry={row.get(\"expiry\")}")
'
```

The output has one line per matching token: its name, its full permission list, and its expiry.

## Notes

- **Wildcard and admin tokens also match.** A `db:*:...` token has read+write on `sensor_data` too. To see only tokens scoped to exactly `sensor_data`, remove the `or "*" in names.split(",")` check.
- **Token secrets aren't listed.** The server stores only a hash, so the output shows names and permissions but never the token values.
- **If you filter by a token name** instead, pass the name as a bound parameter (`WHERE name = $name` with `"params": {"name": "..."}`). Don't build the query string by concatenation.
- **I haven't run this against your instance,** and I don't have the exact field names from `show tokens --format json` on your version. That's why the script uses the HTTP SQL endpoint, whose columns I could confirm. If `expiry` doesn't exist on your version, remove it from the query.

Here's how to do it with the `influxdb3` CLI and `jq`.

**1. List all tokens** (you need an admin token for this):

```bash
influxdb3 show tokens --token "$INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN"

# JSON output, easier to parse in scripts
influxdb3 show tokens --format json --token "$INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN"
```

This command reads from the `system.tokens` table. The `permissions` column comes back as a JSON-encoded string, such as `"[\"db:sensor_data:read\", \"db:sensor_data:write\"]"`, so you have to decode it before filtering.

**2. Keep only the tokens with read and write on `sensor_data`:**

```bash
influxdb3 show tokens --format json --token "$INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN" \
| jq -r --arg db sensor_data '
    .[]
    | . as $t
    | ($t.permissions | if type == "string" then fromjson else . end) as $perms
    # collect every action granted on this db, from any matching permission string
    | [ $perms[]
        | split(":")
        | select(.[0] == "db" or .[0] == "*")
        | select((.[1] | split(",")) as $names | ($names | index($db)) or ($names | index("*")))
        | .[2] | split(",")[]
      ] as $acts
    | select(($acts | index("read") or index("*")) and ($acts | index("write") or index("*")))
    | $t.name'
```

The filter matches all the ways a token can end up with read and write on the database:
- One string: `db:sensor_data:read,write`
- Two strings: `db:sensor_data:read` plus `db:sensor_data:write`
- A list of databases: `db:sensor_data,metrics:read,write`
- Wildcards: `db:*:read,write`, and `*:*:*` for admin tokens

If you only want tokens that name `sensor_data` explicitly, drop the two `index("*")` checks.

**Caveats:**
- **Check the field names first.** I haven't seen the JSON from your instance, so run `influxdb3 show tokens --format json ... | jq '.[0]'` once. If the name or permissions keys differ from `name` and `permissions`, change them in the filter.
- **InfluxDB 3 Core has no scoped tokens.** Every Core token is an admin token with full access to every database, so on Core the filter just returns all your tokens. Scoped `db:<name>:read,write` tokens only exist on InfluxDB 3 Enterprise and InfluxDB 3 Cloud.
- **Keep the admin token out of your shell history.** Read it from an env var or a secret manager rather than pasting it into the command.

If you'd rather use SQL, you can query `SELECT name, permissions FROM system.tokens` against `_internal`. `LIKE` matching on the permissions string will miss the wildcard and multi-database forms, though, which is why I used `jq` above.

Here's how to do it with curl and `jq`. Run it with an admin token, because regular tokens can't read the token list.

### 1. List all tokens

Using the CLI:

```bash
influxdb3 show tokens --token "$INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN"
```

Using the HTTP API, which gives JSON that's easy to filter. Tokens are stored in the `system.tokens` table of the `_internal` database:

```bash
curl -s -X POST "$INFLUXDB_HOST/api/v3/query_sql" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"db": "_internal", "q": "SELECT name, permissions FROM system.tokens"}'
```

The same query in SQL is `SELECT * FROM system.tokens;`. Only the token's name and permissions are shown; the server can't show a token's secret again after it's created.

### 2. Filter to tokens with read and write on `sensor_data`

The `permissions` column is a string that holds a JSON list, such as `["db:sensor_data:read", "db:sensor_data:write"]`. You have to decode that string before you can filter on it. Permissions can also be written as `db:sensor_data:read,write`, `db:sensor_data,metrics:read,write`, or with a `*` wildcard. The filter below handles all of these:

```bash
curl -s -X POST "$INFLUXDB_HOST/api/v3/query_sql" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"db": "_internal", "q": "SELECT name, permissions FROM system.tokens"}' \
| jq --arg db sensor_data '
  map(select(
    (.permissions // "[]" | if type == "string" then fromjson else . end) as $perms
    | [ $perms[]
        | split(":")
        | select(.[0] == "db" or .[0] == "*")
        | select(.[1] | split(",") | (index($db) or index("*")))
        | .[2] | split(",")[]
      ] as $actions
    | (($actions | index("read")) and ($actions | index("write"))) or ($actions | index("*"))
  ))
  | .[].name'
```

For each token, the filter:
1. Decodes the `permissions` string into a list.
2. Keeps permissions whose type is `db` (or `*`) and whose database list includes `sensor_data` (or `*`).
3. Collects the allowed actions from those permissions.
4. Keeps the token only if the actions include both `read` and `write` (or `*`).

The result also includes tokens that get access through wildcards, such as `db:*:read,write` or admin-style `*:*:*`. Those can read and write `sensor_data` too, so they belong in an audit. If you only want tokens that name `sensor_data` directly, remove `or index("*")` from both places. Remove `| .[].name` to see the full rows.

### Notes

- **InfluxDB 3 Core** only has admin tokens, with no per-database permissions. Every token can already read and write every database, so this filter only tells you something on **Enterprise** or **InfluxDB 3 Cloud**.
- **Don't hard-code the token.** Set `INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN` and `INFLUXDB_HOST` as environment variables.
- **To look up one token by name** in a script, pass the name as a parameter instead of pasting it into the query text. Token names are chosen by users, so pasting them in risks SQL injection:
  ```json
  {"db": "_internal", "q": "SELECT name, permissions FROM system.tokens WHERE name = $name", "params": {"name": "my-app"}}
  ```

I haven't run this against your server. If `show tokens --format json` or the query returns something that doesn't look like what's described above, paste the output with any secrets removed and I'll adjust the filter.

graders.evidence:
I've written the script below; save it as `rotate_token.py`. I haven't run it against a live server.

A single command can't guarantee zero downtime, because your app has to pick up the new token between creating it and revoking the old one. So the script works in two steps:

1. **`create`** reads the old token's permissions from `system.tokens` and creates a new token with the same permissions. It checks that the new token works, then saves it to your secret file. The old token keeps working.
2. You restart or roll out your app so it reads the new secret.
3. **`revoke`** checks that the new token has the same permissions and that the saved secret works. It asks you to confirm, then deletes the old token.

### `rotate_token.py`

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Rotate an InfluxDB 3 Enterprise scoped (resource) token without downtime.

Two phases, because consumers must pick up the new secret in between:

  create  Copy the old token's permissions onto a new token, verify it, and
          store its secret. The old token keeps working.
  revoke  Once every consumer runs on the new secret, re-verify it and delete
          the old token.

  python rotate_token.py create --old-name myapp --secret-file ./secrets/influxdb_token
  # ...restart / roll out consumers so they read the new secret...
  python rotate_token.py revoke --old-name myapp --new-name myapp-20260928T120000Z \
      --secret-file ./secrets/influxdb_token

Requires InfluxDB 3 Enterprise or InfluxDB 3 Cloud; Core has no scoped tokens.
Authenticates with INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN, never the app's own INFLUXDB_TOKEN.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import os
import re
import sys
import tempfile
from datetime import datetime, timezone

import requests
from dotenv import load_dotenv

TIMEOUT = 10
STAMP_SUFFIX = re.compile(r"-\d{8}T\d{6}Z$")


class RotationError(RuntimeError):
    pass


def _auth(token: str) -> dict:
    return {"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"}


def check_server(host: str, admin_token: str) -> None:
    r = requests.get(f"{host}/ping", headers=_auth(admin_token), timeout=TIMEOUT)
    if r.status_code == 401:
        raise RotationError("/ping returned 401: INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN is invalid.")
    r.raise_for_status()
    if "core" in r.headers.get("x-influxdb-build", "").lower():
        raise RotationError(
            "This is InfluxDB 3 Core, which has no scoped tokens. "
            "Rotate a named admin token instead (POST /api/v3/configure/token/named_admin)."
        )


def get_token_row(host: str, admin_token: str, name: str) -> dict | None:
    r = requests.post(
        f"{host}/api/v3/query_sql",
        headers={**_auth(admin_token), "Content-Type": "application/json"},
        json={
            "db": "_internal",
            # Bind the name; never interpolate it into the SQL.
            "q": "SELECT name, permissions, expiry FROM system.tokens WHERE name = $name",
            "params": {"name": name},
        },
        timeout=TIMEOUT,
    )
    r.raise_for_status()
    rows = [row for row in r.json() if row.get("name") == name]
    return rows[0] if rows else None


def to_structured(permissions) -> list[dict]:
    """Convert system.tokens short-form perms ("db:x:read") to the create-body form."""
    if isinstance(permissions, str):
        permissions = json.loads(permissions)
    grouped: dict[tuple, set] = {}
    for perm in permissions:
        rtype, names, actions = perm.split(":", 2)
        if rtype not in ("db", "system"):
            raise RotationError(f"Unexpected permission {perm!r}; is this an admin token?")
        key = (rtype, tuple(sorted(names.split(","))))
        grouped.setdefault(key, set()).update(actions.split(","))
    if not grouped:
        raise RotationError("Token has no permissions; refusing to rotate.")
    return [
        {"resource_type": t, "resource_names": list(n), "actions": sorted(a)}
        for (t, n), a in sorted(grouped.items())
    ]


def check_databases_exist(host: str, admin_token: str, perms: list[dict]) -> None:
    r = requests.get(
        f"{host}/api/v3/configure/database",
        params={"format": "json"},
        headers=_auth(admin_token),
        timeout=TIMEOUT,
    )
    r.raise_for_status()
    existing = {row["iox::database"] for row in r.json()}
    missing = [
        n for p in perms if p["resource_type"] == "db"
        for n in p["resource_names"] if n != "*" and n not in existing
    ]
    if missing:
        raise RotationError(f"Token references databases that don't exist: {missing}")


def create_scoped_token(host: str, admin_token: str, name: str,
                        perms: list[dict], expiry_secs: int | None) -> str:
    body = {"type": "resource", "token_name": name, "permissions": perms}
    if expiry_secs:
        body["expiry_secs"] = expiry_secs
    r = requests.post(
        f"{host}/api/v3/enterprise/configure/token",
        headers={**_auth(admin_token), "Content-Type": "application/json"},
        json=body,
        timeout=TIMEOUT,
    )
    if r.status_code == 404:
        raise RotationError("Resource-token endpoint not found; this product doesn't support scoped tokens.")
    if r.status_code == 409:
        raise RotationError(f"A token named {name!r} already exists.")
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()["token"]  # Shown once; the server can't return it again.


def delete_token(host: str, admin_token: str, name: str) -> None:
    r = requests.delete(
        f"{host}/api/v3/configure/token",
        params={"token_name": name},
        headers=_auth(admin_token),
        timeout=TIMEOUT,
    )
    if r.status_code not in (200, 204, 404):
        r.raise_for_status()


def verify_token(host: str, token: str, perms: list[dict]) -> None:
    """Probe read access with the token itself. Write-only perms can't be probed safely."""
    probed = 0
    for p in perms:
        if p["resource_type"] != "db" or "read" not in p["actions"]:
            continue
        for db in p["resource_names"]:
            if db == "*":
                continue
            r = requests.post(
                f"{host}/api/v3/query_sql",
                headers={**_auth(token), "Content-Type": "application/json"},
                json={"db": db, "q": "SELECT 1"},
                timeout=TIMEOUT,
            )
            if r.status_code != 200:
                raise RotationError(f"New token failed a read probe on {db!r}: HTTP {r.status_code}")
            probed += 1
    if not probed:
        print("  warning: no readable database to probe; verify the new token manually.")


def store_secret(path: str, secret: str) -> None:
    """Atomically write the secret with 0600 permissions.

    Replace this with your secret manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, k8s Secret, ...).
    """
    directory = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(path))
    fd, tmp = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=directory, prefix=".influxdb-token-")  # mode 0600
    try:
        with os.fdopen(fd, "w") as f:
            f.write(secret)
        os.replace(tmp, path)
    except BaseException:
        if os.path.exists(tmp):
            os.unlink(tmp)
        raise


def cmd_create(host: str, admin_token: str, args) -> int:
    check_server(host, admin_token)
    old = get_token_row(host, admin_token, args.old_name)
    if old is None:
        raise RotationError(f"No token named {args.old_name!r}.")
    perms = to_structured(old["permissions"])
    check_databases_exist(host, admin_token, perms)

    base = STAMP_SUFFIX.sub("", args.old_name)
    new_name = f"{base}-{datetime.now(timezone.utc):%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ}"
    expiry_secs = args.expiry_days * 86400 if args.expiry_days else None

    print(f"==> creating {new_name} with {perms}")
    secret = create_scoped_token(host, admin_token, new_name, perms, expiry_secs)
    try:
        print("==> verifying new token")
        verify_token(host, secret, perms)
        print(f"==> storing secret in {args.secret_file}")
        store_secret(args.secret_file, secret)
    except BaseException:
        # The secret never reached consumers, so the new token is useless; remove it.
        delete_token(host, admin_token, new_name)
        raise

    print(f"\nDone. {args.old_name!r} still works. Next:")
    print("  1. Restart or roll out every consumer so it reads the new secret.")
    print(f"  2. python {sys.argv[0]} revoke --old-name {args.old_name} "
          f"--new-name {new_name} --secret-file {args.secret_file}")
    return 0


def cmd_revoke(host: str, admin_token: str, args) -> int:
    if args.old_name == args.new_name:
        raise RotationError("--old-name and --new-name are the same.")
    check_server(host, admin_token)

    new = get_token_row(host, admin_token, args.new_name)
    if new is None:
        raise RotationError(f"New token {args.new_name!r} not found; not revoking anything.")
    old = get_token_row(host, admin_token, args.old_name)
    if old is None:
        print(f"{args.old_name!r} is already gone.")
        return 0

    perms = to_structured(new["permissions"])
    if perms != to_structured(old["permissions"]):
        raise RotationError("Old and new tokens have different permissions; refusing to revoke.")

    with open(args.secret_file) as f:
        secret = f.read().strip()
    print("==> verifying the secret consumers will read")
    verify_token(host, secret, perms)

    if not args.yes:
        answer = input(f"Every consumer is running on {args.new_name!r}? Delete {args.old_name!r} [y/N] ")
        if answer.strip().lower() != "y":
            print("Aborted; nothing deleted.")
            return 1

    print(f"==> deleting {args.old_name}")
    delete_token(host, admin_token, args.old_name)
    print("Done. Rotation complete.")
    return 0


def main() -> int:
    load_dotenv()
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__, formatter_class=argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter)
    sub = parser.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)

    c = sub.add_parser("create", help="create and store a replacement token")
    c.add_argument("--old-name", required=True)
    c.add_argument("--secret-file", required=True)
    c.add_argument("--expiry-days", type=int, help="optional expiry for the new token")

    r = sub.add_parser("revoke", help="delete the old token after consumers switched")
    r.add_argument("--old-name", required=True)
    r.add_argument("--new-name", required=True)
    r.add_argument("--secret-file", required=True)
    r.add_argument("--yes", action="store_true", help="skip the confirmation prompt (CI)")

    args = parser.parse_args()
    try:
        host = os.environ["INFLUXDB_HOST"].rstrip("/")
        admin_token = os.environ["INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN"]
    except KeyError as e:
        print(f"error: {e.args[0]} is not set", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2

    try:
        return (cmd_create if args.command == "create" else cmd_revoke)(host, admin_token, args)
    except (RotationError, requests.RequestException, OSError) as e:
        print(f"error: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())
```

### Supporting files

`requirements.txt`
```
requests>=2.31
python-dotenv>=1.0
```

`.env.example` (commit this file, not `.env`)
```
INFLUXDB_HOST=http://localhost:8181
INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN=
```

`.gitignore`
```
.env
secrets/
```

### Before you run it

- **Product:** this needs InfluxDB 3 Enterprise or InfluxDB 3 Cloud. InfluxDB 3 Core has no scoped tokens, and the script stops if it detects Core. On Core you'd rotate a named admin token instead.
- **Admin token:** set `INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN` to an admin token. The script never uses the app's `INFLUXDB_TOKEN`, because a scoped token can't create or delete tokens.
- **Where the secret goes:** `store_secret()` writes a file readable only by you. If you use Vault, AWS Secrets Manager or a Kubernetes Secret, replace that function's body; nothing else needs to change. The new secret is never printed, so it won't end up in CI logs.
- **Restart between steps:** clients that stay running keep using the token they started with until they restart or reconnect. Only run `revoke` once every instance has restarted.

### Limitations

- **Revoke can't tell old from new secret:** InfluxDB doesn't show which token a client is using. If your secret file still holds the old secret, the check in `revoke` passes anyway, which is why it asks you to confirm. Check your app's logs or restart status before answering yes.
- **Write-only tokens aren't tested:** the check runs a read query, `SELECT 1`, against each database the token can read. A write-only token gets a warning, not a test, because testing a write would add real data.
- **Expiry isn't copied:** the new token has no expiry unless you pass `--expiry-days`.
- **Failed `create` is undone:** if saving or checking the new token fails, the script deletes it again and the old token stays in place.

1. **`rotate`**: looks up the current token's permissions and creates a new token with the same permissions. It checks that the new token works, then saves its secret to your secret store. If the check or the save fails, it deletes the new token, and the old one keeps working.
2. **You:** restart or roll every app instance so it reads the new secret.
3. **`revoke`**: checks that the secret store holds a *different*, working token. It then asks you to confirm and deletes the old token.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Zero-downtime rotation of an InfluxDB 3 Enterprise / InfluxDB 3 Cloud scoped token.

Two phases, so no consumer ever holds a revoked token:

  rotate  create a new token with the old token's permissions, verify it,
          and write its secret to the secret store. The old token stays valid.
  (you)   roll/restart every consumer so it picks up the new secret.
  revoke  verify the stored secret works and isn't the old token, then delete
          the old token.

InfluxDB 3 Core has no resource tokens; this script refuses to run against it.

Env:
  INFLUXDB_HOST         e.g. https://influxdb.example.com:8181
  INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN  admin token used to create/delete tokens (never the app's token)
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import os
import sys
import time
from collections import defaultdict
from datetime import datetime, timezone

import requests
from dotenv import dotenv_values, load_dotenv

TIMEOUT = 10
VERIFY_ATTEMPTS = 5  # new tokens may take a moment to reach every node


class RotationError(RuntimeError):
    pass


# --- InfluxDB admin API -----------------------------------------------------

class Influx:
    def __init__(self, host: str, admin_token: str):
        self.host = host.rstrip("/")
        self.admin_token = admin_token

    def _headers(self, token: str | None = None) -> dict:
        return {"Authorization": f"Bearer {token or self.admin_token}"}

    def assert_supports_scoped_tokens(self) -> None:
        r = requests.get(f"{self.host}/ping", headers=self._headers(), timeout=TIMEOUT)
        if r.status_code == 401:
            raise RotationError("INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN was rejected (401).")
        r.raise_for_status()
        build = r.headers.get("x-influxdb-build", "").lower()
        if "core" in build:
            raise RotationError(
                "Server is InfluxDB 3 Core, which has no scoped resource tokens. "
                "Rotate the app's named admin token instead."
            )
        if "enterprise" not in build:
            print(f"warning: unrecognized build header {build!r}; assuming Enterprise-compatible API")

    def list_databases(self) -> set[str]:
        r = requests.get(
            f"{self.host}/api/v3/configure/database",
            params={"format": "json"},
            headers=self._headers(),
            timeout=TIMEOUT,
        )
        r.raise_for_status()
        return {row["iox::database"] for row in r.json()}

    def get_token(self, name: str) -> dict | None:
        r = requests.post(
            f"{self.host}/api/v3/query_sql",
            headers=self._headers(),
            json={
                "db": "_internal",
                "q": "SELECT name, permissions, expiry FROM system.tokens WHERE name = $name",
                "params": {"name": name},  # bound, never interpolated
            },
            timeout=TIMEOUT,
        )
        r.raise_for_status()
        rows = [row for row in r.json() if row.get("name") == name]
        return rows[0] if rows else None

    def create_scoped_token(self, name: str, permissions: list[dict], expiry_secs: int | None) -> str:
        body = {"type": "resource", "token_name": name, "permissions": permissions}
        if expiry_secs:
            body["expiry_secs"] = expiry_secs
        r = requests.post(
            f"{self.host}/api/v3/enterprise/configure/token",
            headers=self._headers(),
            json=body,
            timeout=TIMEOUT,
        )
        if r.status_code == 409:
            raise RotationError(f"a token named {name!r} already exists")
        r.raise_for_status()
        return r.json()["token"]  # plaintext is returned once; never logged

    def delete_token(self, name: str) -> None:
        r = requests.delete(
            f"{self.host}/api/v3/configure/token",
            params={"token_name": name},
            headers=self._headers(),
            timeout=TIMEOUT,
        )
        if r.status_code not in (200, 204, 404):
            r.raise_for_status()

    def verify_token(self, secret: str, permissions: list[dict]) -> None:
        """Run a read-only query with the token on every concrete DB it can read."""
        readable = [
            db
            for p in permissions
            if p["resource_type"] == "db" and "read" in p["actions"]
            for db in p["resource_names"]
            if db != "*"
        ]
        if not readable:
            print("warning: token has no read scope on a named database; skipping live check")
            return
        for db in readable:
            for attempt in range(1, VERIFY_ATTEMPTS + 1):
                r = requests.post(
                    f"{self.host}/api/v3/query_sql",
                    headers=self._headers(secret),
                    json={"db": db, "q": "SELECT 1"},
                    timeout=TIMEOUT,
                )
                if r.status_code == 200:
                    break
                if attempt == VERIFY_ATTEMPTS:
                    raise RotationError(
                        f"token failed read check on {db!r}: HTTP {r.status_code} {r.text[:200]}"
                    )
                time.sleep(2 * attempt)
            print(f"  verified read on {db!r}")


def parse_permissions(raw: str) -> list[dict]:
    """system.tokens stores e.g. '["db:sensors:read","db:sensors:write"]'.
    Convert to the structured form the create-token API expects."""
    grouped: dict[tuple, set] = defaultdict(set)
    for perm in json.loads(raw):
        rtype, names, actions = perm.split(":", 2)
        if rtype not in ("db", "system") or not set(actions.split(",")) <= {"read", "write"}:
            raise RotationError(
                f"permission {perm!r} isn't a resource-token permission; "
                "this script only rotates scoped tokens"
            )
        grouped[(rtype, tuple(sorted(names.split(","))))].update(actions.split(","))
    return [
        {"resource_type": rtype, "resource_names": list(names), "actions": sorted(actions)}
        for (rtype, names), actions in grouped.items()
    ]


# --- Secret stores ------------------------------------------------------------
# Both stores keep INFLUXDB_TOKEN (the secret the app reads) and
# INFLUXDB_TOKEN_NAME (so `revoke` can tell which token is live).

class AwsSecretStore:
    """AWS Secrets Manager secret holding a JSON object. Other keys are preserved,
    and the previous version stays available as AWSPREVIOUS for rollback."""

    def __init__(self, secret_id: str):
        import boto3

        self.client = boto3.client("secretsmanager")
        self.secret_id = secret_id

    def _load(self) -> dict:
        resp = self.client.get_secret_value(SecretId=self.secret_id)
        return json.loads(resp["SecretString"])

    def read(self) -> tuple[str | None, str | None]:
        data = self._load()
        return data.get("INFLUXDB_TOKEN"), data.get("INFLUXDB_TOKEN_NAME")

    def write(self, token: str, name: str) -> None:
        data = self._load()
        data.update({"INFLUXDB_TOKEN": token, "INFLUXDB_TOKEN_NAME": name})
        self.client.put_secret_value(SecretId=self.secret_id, SecretString=json.dumps(data))


class EnvFileStore:
    """A .env-style file the app loads. Written atomically with mode 0600."""

    def __init__(self, path: str):
        self.path = path

    def read(self) -> tuple[str | None, str | None]:
        values = dotenv_values(self.path)
        return values.get("INFLUXDB_TOKEN"), values.get("INFLUXDB_TOKEN_NAME")

    def write(self, token: str, name: str) -> None:
        updates = {"INFLUXDB_TOKEN": token, "INFLUXDB_TOKEN_NAME": name}
        lines = open(self.path).read().splitlines() if os.path.exists(self.path) else []
        out, seen = [], set()
        for line in lines:
            key = line.split("=", 1)[0].strip()
            if key in updates:
                out.append(f"{key}={updates[key]}")
                seen.add(key)
            else:
                out.append(line)
        out += [f"{k}={v}" for k, v in updates.items() if k not in seen]
        tmp = f"{self.path}.tmp"
        fd = os.open(tmp, os.O_WRONLY | os.O_CREAT | os.O_TRUNC, 0o600)
        with os.fdopen(fd, "w") as f:
            f.write("\n".join(out) + "\n")
        os.replace(tmp, self.path)


# --- Phases -------------------------------------------------------------------

def rotate(influx: Influx, store, app: str, old_name: str, expiry_days: int | None) -> None:
    old = influx.get_token(old_name)
    if old is None:
        raise RotationError(f"current token {old_name!r} not found")
    permissions = parse_permissions(old["permissions"])

    # A token scoped to a missing database usually means a typo or a renamed DB.
    missing = {
        db
        for p in permissions
        if p["resource_type"] == "db"
        for db in p["resource_names"]
        if db != "*"
    } - influx.list_databases()
    if missing:
        raise RotationError(f"token is scoped to databases that don't exist: {sorted(missing)}")

    new_name = f"{app}_{datetime.now(timezone.utc):%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ}"
    print(f"==> creating {new_name!r} with permissions {permissions}")
    secret = influx.create_scoped_token(
        new_name, permissions, expiry_days * 86400 if expiry_days else None
    )

    try:
        print("==> verifying new token")
        influx.verify_token(secret, permissions)
        print("==> writing new token to secret store")
        store.write(secret, new_name)
    except Exception:
        # Old token is untouched, so consumers keep working. Don't orphan the new one.
        print(f"!! rotation failed; deleting {new_name!r}. {old_name!r} remains active.")
        influx.delete_token(new_name)
        raise

    print(
        f"\nDone. New token {new_name!r} is in the secret store; {old_name!r} is still valid.\n"
        "Next: roll/restart every consumer, confirm they're healthy, then run:\n"
        f"  {sys.argv[0]} revoke --old-token-name {old_name} ..."
    )


def revoke(influx: Influx, store, old_name: str, assume_yes: bool) -> None:
    stored_secret, stored_name = store.read()
    if not stored_secret or not stored_name:
        raise RotationError("secret store has no INFLUXDB_TOKEN / INFLUXDB_TOKEN_NAME")
    if stored_name == old_name:
        raise RotationError(f"secret store still points at {old_name!r}; run `rotate` first")

    live = influx.get_token(stored_name)
    if live is None:
        raise RotationError(f"token in secret store ({stored_name!r}) doesn't exist on the server")
    print(f"==> verifying stored token {stored_name!r}")
    influx.verify_token(stored_secret, parse_permissions(live["permissions"]))

    if influx.get_token(old_name) is None:
        print(f"{old_name!r} is already gone; nothing to revoke.")
        return

    if not assume_yes:
        answer = input(
            f"Have ALL consumers restarted onto {stored_name!r}? "
            f"Revoking {old_name!r} breaks any that haven't. [y/N] "
        )
        if answer.strip().lower() != "y":
            print("Aborted; nothing revoked.")
            return

    print(f"==> deleting {old_name!r}")
    influx.delete_token(old_name)
    if influx.get_token(old_name) is not None:
        raise RotationError(f"{old_name!r} still listed after delete")
    print("Done. Old token revoked.")


def main() -> int:
    load_dotenv()
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__, formatter_class=argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter)
    ap.add_argument("--store", choices=["aws", "file"], required=True)
    ap.add_argument("--secret-id", help="AWS Secrets Manager secret ID (--store aws)")
    ap.add_argument("--env-file", help="path to the app's env file (--store file)")
    sub = ap.add_subparsers(dest="phase", required=True)

    r = sub.add_parser("rotate", help="create + verify + store the new token")
    r.add_argument("--app", required=True, help="prefix for the new token name")
    r.add_argument("--old-token-name", default=os.environ.get("INFLUXDB_TOKEN_NAME"))
    r.add_argument("--expiry-days", type=int, help="optional expiry for the new token")

    v = sub.add_parser("revoke", help="delete the old token after consumers have switched")
    v.add_argument("--old-token-name", required=True)
    v.add_argument("--yes", action="store_true", help="skip the confirmation prompt (CI)")

    args = ap.parse_args()

    if args.store == "aws":
        if not args.secret_id:
            ap.error("--secret-id is required with --store aws")
        store = AwsSecretStore(args.secret_id)
    else:
        if not args.env_file:
            ap.error("--env-file is required with --store file")
        store = EnvFileStore(args.env_file)

    try:
        influx = Influx(os.environ["INFLUXDB_HOST"], os.environ["INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN"])
    except KeyError as exc:
        ap.error(f"missing env var {exc}")

    try:
        influx.assert_supports_scoped_tokens()
        if args.phase == "rotate":
            if not args.old_token_name:
                ap.error("--old-token-name (or INFLUXDB_TOKEN_NAME) is required")
            rotate(influx, store, args.app, args.old_token_name, args.expiry_days)
        else:
            revoke(influx, store, args.old_token_name, args.yes)
        return 0
    except (RotationError, requests.HTTPError) as exc:
        print(f"error: {exc}", file=sys.stderr)
        return 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())
```

## Usage

```bash
# 1. Create the new token, check it, and save it. The old token keeps working.
python rotate_influxdb_token.py --store aws --secret-id prod/myapp/influxdb \
  rotate --app myapp --old-token-name myapp_20260601T000000Z

# 2. Restart or roll your app instances and confirm they're healthy.

# 3. Delete the old token.
python rotate_influxdb_token.py --store aws --secret-id prod/myapp/influxdb \
  revoke --old-token-name myapp_20260601T000000Z
```

## Before running
- **The server is reachable:** `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN" $INFLUXDB_HOST/ping` should return 200 with an `x-influxdb-build` header that says Enterprise.
- **Two tokens:** `INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN` is the admin token the script uses to create and delete tokens. Your app keeps reading its own scoped `INFLUXDB_TOKEN` and never sees the admin token. In CI, pass the admin token as a masked secret, not through a committed file.
- **The old token has a name:** find it with `influxdb3 show tokens --token "$INFLUXDB_ADMIN_TOKEN"`. After the first run, the script also saves `INFLUXDB_TOKEN_NAME` in the secret store.
- **`.gitignore` covers `.env`** before you use `--store file` with a local env file.

## Things to know
- **Only `rotate` → restart → `revoke` avoids downtime.** Any app instance that still holds the old token when you run `revoke` will start getting 401 errors. Long-lived clients keep using the token they were started with, so a restart is required, not optional.
- **The check is read-only.** The script runs `SELECT 1` against each database the token can read, so it adds no test data. For a write-only token, or one scoped with `db:*`, the live check is skipped and a warning is printed.
- **The secret is never printed.** The server returns it once when the token is created. If saving it to the store fails, the script deletes the new token instead of leaving an unusable one behind.
- **Rollback:** with AWS Secrets Manager, the previous value stays available as `AWSPREVIOUS` until you run `revoke`.
- **Not tested:** I haven't run this against a live server. The endpoints and response shapes come from the InfluxDB 3 Enterprise admin API reference. Try it once on a staging instance before using it in production.
